title: Electric power as a system: Edison DC central station, Westinghouse AC and Niagara scale transition
pressure: Electric lighting had to compete with gas as a reliable service, not merely a laboratory lamp. A useful public power system required generation, conductors, lamps, meters, switching/protection, distribution economics and an architecture whose voltage/current choices determined reachable distance and load class.
preExistingWorldModel: Arc lighting and generators existed. Edison pursued a low-voltage DC lighting system for dense local districts; Westinghouse and others developed transformer AC for greater distribution distance. The contest mixed technical tradeoffs, patents, economics and safety/public legitimacy rather than one device.
candidateRoutes: polyphase AC generation/transmission for larger hydro/industrial systems
observationsAndInstruments: Edison and collaborators developed lamp, generator, feeder/main distribution, meter and station-control components as one service architecture; Pearl Street began service in September 1882.
Pearl Street supplied a roughly half-mile local area at low-voltage DC, making load density and conductor economics part of the architecture.
Westinghouse adopted transformer-based AC distribution during the mid-1880s, allowing voltage to rise for transmission and fall near customers.

Niagara selected polyphase AC; Westinghouse generators began operation in 1895 and transmission to Buffalo followed in 1896, moving the demonstrated scale from neighborhood station to regional system.
decisiveTests: A lamp had to survive repeated customer use inside a complete service, not only glow in an experiment.
Central-station economics depended on the number/density of paying loads reachable before conductor losses and copper cost dominated.
AC had to demonstrate controllable transformation and useful customer service, not merely high voltage.
Niagara tested generation, polyphase machinery and transmission together at much greater power/distance than Pearl Street.
technicalOrScientificTransition: Electricity changed from local machines/demonstrations into infrastructure binding generation, distribution distance, customer loads and operating standards. Regional AC scale did not make Pearl Street unreal; it changed applicability and economics.
rivalsAndFailures: Pearl Street was a real local technical success but low-voltage DC had a short economic radius.
AC/DC safety controversy mixed genuine hazards with commercial/patent conflict.
Early central-station business economics were not automatically attractive when apparatus worked.
Later motor/factory loads changed the value surface beyond Edison's original lighting objective.
diffusionAndScaling: Central stations proliferated; transformer AC increasingly served larger areas and loads. Niagara became a high-visibility demonstration of hydro generation plus long-distance polyphase power.
standardsAndInstitutions: Utilities, patent firms, municipal franchises, equipment vendors and emerging electrical standards bodies held distinct responsibilities.
externalitiesAndCorrections: Dense wiring/high voltage introduced fire and electrocution risks requiring protection practice and later codes; utility scale concentrated infrastructural authority.
secondOrderEffects: A reusable power substrate opened motors, transport, electrochemistry, communications and new factory layouts.
sourceNativeSummary: The transition is not one winning current. Pearl Street shows that useful electricity required a complete local service architecture; transformer AC changed feasible distribution radius; Niagara tested a larger coupled system. Later scale should not retroactively erase scoped DC success.
unresolvedHistoricalQuestions: How much of AC's pre-1896 advantage came from conductor economics versus motors, patents/business structure and expected future scale?
Which safety differences were intrinsic to architecture versus installation practice/public persuasion?
